description: Feed your sourdough starter at 1:1:1, 1:2:2, or 1:5:5. Work out the flour and water for any amount of starter, with the ratio table and timing notes.

examples.result: Feed 30 g starter with 60 g flour and 60 g water. Total starter 150 g.
steps: The ratio is 1:2:2, so flour and water are each twice the starter.
examples.title: Feed 30 g starter at 1:2:2

examples.result: Feed 20 g starter with 100 g flour and 100 g water. Total starter 220 g.
steps: The ratio is 1:5:5, so flour and water are each five times the starter.
examples.title: Feed 20 g starter at 1:5:5

examples.result: Keep 40 g starter and feed it 80 g flour and 80 g water. Total starter 200 g.
steps: You need 200 g of starter for the recipe, and you want to build it from a small amount you keep.
At 1:2:2, the total is 5 parts: 1 part starter, 2 parts flour, 2 parts water.
Starter to keep: 40 g. Flour: 40 × 2 = 80 g. Water: 40 × 2 = 80 g.
examples.title: Build 200 g of starter for bake day

faqs.answer: The three numbers are starter, flour, and water, by weight. A 1:2:2 feeding gives one part starter, two parts flour, and two parts water. So 30 g of starter takes 60 g of flour and 60 g of water. Equal parts flour and water keep the starter at 100% hydration.
faqs.question: What does 1:2:2 mean?

faqs.answer: A bigger feeding takes longer to peak, because the yeast and bacteria have more fresh flour to work through. A 1:1:1 feeding peaks fastest, often in a few hours in a warm kitchen. A 1:5:5 feeding is the slowest, which makes it the right choice for an overnight build or a starter that lives in the fridge.
faqs.question: Which ratio should I use before baking?

faqs.answer: Yes, if you feed it first. A starter that has been in the fridge for a week is sleepy, not dead. Give it a 1:2:2 feeding, leave it at room temperature, and it should be bubbly and doubled by the next day. If it is sluggish after two feedings, a spoonful of whole wheat or rye flour in the feeding usually wakes it up.
faqs.question: Can I use starter straight from the fridge?

faqs.answer: It is ready when it has roughly doubled, is domed on top, and is full of bubbles, and it smells pleasantly tangy rather than sharply acidic. If it has risen and fallen back, with a layer of dark liquid on top, it is hungry: feed it again and use it at the next peak.
faqs.question: How do I know my starter is ready to bake with?

faqs.answer: A high ratio like 1:5:5 makes a milder starter, because the small amount of old starter is diluted in a lot of fresh flour and the acids build up more slowly. A low ratio like 1:1:1 keeps more of the old starter in the mix and gives a tangier loaf. If your bread is too sour, feed at a higher ratio for a few days before baking.
faqs.question: Does the feeding ratio change how sour my bread is?

felicityNote: I keep a small starter, about 30 grams, and feed it 1:2:2 the night before a bake. A small starter wastes less flour and still makes plenty for a loaf.

parts.meaning: The ripe starter you keep from the jar, in grams. This is the 1 in the ratio.
Fresh flour to add. At 1:2:2 it is twice the starter; at 1:5:5 it is five times.
Fresh water to add. Always the same weight as the flour, so the starter stays at 100% hydration.
Starter, flour, and water after feeding. At 1:2:2, the total is five times the starter you kept.

formula.text: Flour = starter × the middle number. Water = starter × the last number. Total starter = starter + flour + water.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the starter to keep
howToSteps.text: Put a clean jar on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the starter you are keeping. Discard the rest, or use it in pancakes, crackers, or waffles.

howToSteps.name: Add the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Weigh in the flour and water from the calculator. Use the same weight of each to keep the starter at 100% hydration.

howToSteps.name: Mix and mark
howToSteps.text: Stir until no dry flour is left, scrape down the sides, and mark the level with a rubber band or a piece of tape. The mark shows you how far it rises.

howToSteps.name: Leave it to peak
howToSteps.text: Cover loosely and leave at room temperature. A 1:1:1 feeding peaks fastest, a 1:5:5 feeding slowest. Use the starter when it has doubled and is domed and bubbly.

lede: Feeding a starter is just three numbers: the starter you keep, and equal weights of fresh flour and water. Pick a ratio, weigh it, and the starter does the rest.

title: Sourdough Starter Feeding Calculator
tutorial: A feeding ratio is three numbers: starter, flour, and water, by weight. A 1:2:2 feeding means one part starter, two parts flour, and two parts water. Keep 30 g of starter, feed it 60 g of flour and 60 g of water, and you have 150 g of starter when it peaks. The flour and water are always equal, which keeps the starter at 100% hydration, half flour and half water.

The ratio sets the pace. A 1:1:1 feeding peaks fastest, because the yeast and bacteria have the least fresh flour to work through, so it is the right choice when you want starter ready in a few hours. A 1:2:2 feeding is the everyday middle ground: enough food for a full day at room temperature. A 1:5:5 feeding is the slow one, best for an overnight build or for a starter that is about to go back in the fridge.

The ratio also sets the flavour. A high ratio like 1:5:5 dilutes the old starter in a lot of fresh flour, so the acids build up slowly and the bread comes out milder. A low ratio like 1:1:1 keeps more of the old, acidic starter in the mix and gives a tangier loaf. If your bread is more sour than you like, feed at a higher ratio for a few days before baking and see if it softens.

A small starter wastes less flour. There is no need to keep a litre of starter in the fridge when 30 g, fed 1:2:2, makes 150 g by morning, which is more than most recipes need. Keep it small, feed it the night before a bake, and build up only when the recipe calls for more. The third worked example below shows the build-up maths: to get 200 g of starter, keep 40 g and feed it 1:2:2.

The discard does not have to go in the bin. The starter you do not keep is still flour and water with flavour in it, and it makes good pancakes, waffles, crackers, and flatbreads. If you bake once a week and feed once a week, the discard is small. If you feed every day, the discard adds up fast, and that is the real argument for keeping a small starter.
